stimulus.text: The painting shows the surrender at Yorktown on October 19, 1781. In the center, a British officer in a red coat stands before an American officer on a white horse and presents his sword. American officers on horseback and on foot stand to the right, under the American flag, while British officers wait to the left under a white flag. The painting is John Trumbull's Surrender of Lord Cornwallis, painted in 1820. Cornwallis himself did not attend the surrender; he sent his second-in-command, General Charles O'Hara, who is the British officer shown presenting the sword.

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: What does the painting show about the surrender at Yorktown?

options.text: The French fleet fires on the British from the York River
options.misconception: No fleet or firing is shown; the painting shows the formal surrender on land, under flags of truce.

options.text: American troops storm the British earthworks at Yorktown
options.misconception: The painting shows a formal surrender ceremony, not an assault on earthworks; the siege had already ended.

options.text: A British officer presents his sword while Cornwallis stays away
Cornwallis himself hands his sword to Washington
options.misconception: Cornwallis did not attend the surrender; he sent General O'Hara, who presented the sword in his place.

rationales.C: O'Hara, Cornwallis's second-in-command, presents the sword to the Americans, while Cornwallis himself stayed in his quarters.
rationales.D: Cornwallis did not attend; he claimed illness and sent O'Hara, so the painting shows his deputy, not Cornwallis.
rationales.A: The French fleet's role was to block escape by sea; the painting shows the land surrender, with no ships firing.
rationales.B: The assault on the earthworks came before the surrender; the painting shows the ceremony that followed it.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the center. A British officer in red offers his sword to an American officer on a white horse.
2. Ask who is missing. Cornwallis is not in the painting; he sent O'Hara, his second-in-command, to surrender in his place.
3. Name the scene. A formal, orderly surrender, with officers under flags, not a battle or a bombardment.
Remember: in a surrender painting, ask who is present and who is absent — the absence is part of the story.
